title: Don't lean on mortals
hook: don't rest your hopes on people who cannot save you (Sukhmani 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, siaanap: drop the cleverness and keep one hope. Today the fourteenth ashtpadi's first stanza asks where that hope should rest.

A friend said he'd put in a word for you. He knows the manager. It's basically done, he said. So you stopped applying anywhere else. Two weeks, three weeks. Then a text: so sorry, it didn't work out, they went internal. He meant well. He just couldn't carry what you'd put on him. It's easy to lean your whole weight on somebody like that, a friend, a boss, a parent, a partner, and feel the floor tilt when they can't hold it.
screen: `HE'LL PUT IN A WORD FOR YOU.` → `YOU STOP LOOKING ANYWHERE ELSE.` → `THE FLOOR TILTS.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: know that all reliance on mortals is in vain; the Giver is the One Lord alone. The key word is tek: a prop, a support, like a walking stick or a post you rest your back against. Brithee means useless, in vain. So the human prop won't bear the weight. That could sound bleak, even cold. Don't trust people? But Sikh life doesn't look like that at all. The tradition runs on people: the sangat, the company; the langar, cooked and served by volunteers; families who carry each other for generations. Sukhmani itself, a few days back, told us to take shelter in the company of the good. So the stanza can't mean, have nothing to do with people. It's narrower and kinder. It's about the last weight, the final hope, the thing you'd collapse without. People are limited, not because they're bad, but because they're people. They get sick, they forget, they move away, they die. Your friend couldn't control the manager. When all your hope rests on one person, you've asked them to be something no human can be, and when they fail, you end up resenting them for being human. Lean your final weight on the One, the stanza says, and something surprising happens. You can love people without crushing them. Your friend can be just a friend: a good one, a limited one, and that's enough.
screen: `TEK: THE PROP YOU LEAN ON.` · `NOT: HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH PEOPLE.` · `PEOPLE ARE LIMITED, NOT BAD.` · `LOVE WITHOUT CRUSHING.` · then, large: `LEAN ON THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Let your body lean into the chair, the wall or the floor, and notice what's holding you right now. Then bring to mind one person you've been leaning on very hard, see them kindly as a person with limits, and gently take a little weight off them, letting it rest deeper, wherever you sense something steadier than any one person. If you pray, rest it in Waheguru.
Tek, a prop, a support. Maanukh kee tek, the human prop, can't bear your final weight; Sukhmani says rest that weight in the One.
Your line: lean on the one. Then people can just be people. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: If Sukhmani says relying on people is in vain, should I stop asking friends for help?
options: No. Love and lean on people, but rest your final hope in the One; people are limited, not bad.
Yes, needing help from people shows weak faith, so a true Sikh handles everything alone.
Only trust family; the stanza warns about friends and coworkers, not about relatives.
chat.meaning: The stanza is about the final weight, which the human prop can't bear. Sikh life runs on sangat and langar, so people still matter.
